{{nihongo|'''Minase Shrine'''|水無瀬神宮|Minase jingū}} is a Shinto Shrine in {{ill|Shimamoto, Osaka|en|Shimamoto, Osaka|qid=Q1347149|lt=Shimamoto, Osaka}}<ref name="kanpei-taisha1940">Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' p. 126.</ref>

The Shrine is dedicated to the veneration of the ''kami'' of {{ill|Emperor Go-Toba|en|Emperor Go-Toba|qid=Q316658|lt=Emperor Go-Toba}}, {{ill|Emperor Tsuchimikado|en|Emperor Tsuchimikado|qid=Q357269|lt=Emperor Tsuchimikado}} and {{ill|Emperor Juntoku|en|Emperor Juntoku|qid=Q357249|lt=Emperor Juntoku}}.<ref name="kanpei-taisha1940"/>   In the struggle with the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|qid=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}, the three historical figures are united by one common factor—each was overpowered and banished from the Imperial center in Kyoto: Go-Toba was banished to [[:en:Oki Island|Oki Island]], where he died.<ref>Brownlee, John S. (1991). [https://books.google.com/books?id=P1OZUmnLTdoC&pg=PA104  ''Political Thought in Japanese Historical Writing: From Kojiki (712) to Tokushi Yoron (1712),'' p.104.]</ref> Tsuchimikado felt compelled to abandon Kyoto, traveling first to [[:en:Tosa province|Tosa province]] (now known as {{ill|Kōchi Prefecture|en|Kōchi Prefecture|qid=Q134093|lt=Kōchi Prefecture}}); and later, he removed himself to {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|en|Awa Province (Tokushima)|qid=Q907457|lt=Awa province}}, where he died in exile.<ref>Takekoshi, Yosaburō. (2004). [https://books.google.com/books?id=2ujfVq9v4zoC&pg=PA186  ''The Economic Aspects of the History of the Civilization of Japan,'' Volume 1, p. 186.]</ref> Juntoku was forced to end his days at {{ill|Sado, Niigata|en|Sado, Niigata|qid=Q499047|lt=Sado Island}}.<ref>Bornoff, Nicholas. (2005). ''National Geographic Traveler Japan,'' p. 193.</ref>
In 1873, the ''kami'' of Go-Daigo and Tushimikado were enshrined, and the ''kami'' of Juntoku was enshrined in 1874.<ref>Holton, Daniel Clarence. (1922). [https://books.google.com/books?id=SRwNAAAAYAAJ&dq=minase+jingu&pg=PA273  ''The Political Philosophy of Modern Shintō, a Study of the State Religion of Japan,'' p. 273.]</ref>

==Kanpei-sha==
In 1871, the {{nihongo|''Kanpei-sha''|官幣社}} identified the hierarchy of government-supported shrines most closely associated with the Imperial family.<ref name="imperial124">Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' p. 124.</ref>  The ''kampeisha'' were shrines venerated by the imperial family.  This category encompasses those sanctuaries enshrining emperors, imperial family members, or meritorious retainers of the Imperial family.<ref name="system">Institute for Japanese Culture and Classics, Kokugakuin University: [http://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/ijcc/wp/glossary/def_K.html  Glossary of Shinto Names and Terms, ''Kampei Taisha.'']</ref>  Up through 1940, the mid-range of Imperial shrines or {{nihongo|''Kanpei-chūsha''|官幣中社}} included  the shrine; and it was then known as Minase''-gū''<ref name="imperial125">Ponsonby-Fane. ''Imperial,'' p. 125.</ref> In 1940, Minase's status was changed {{nihongo|''Kanpei-taisha''|官幣大社}}, which is the highest Rank; and since then, it has been known as Minase ''jingū.''<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1963). ''The Vicissitudes of Shinto,'' p. 394.</ref>
